name: Priya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can tell me separately what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. Could you describe your usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, and a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I came into this work after years in a shop, so I'm still slower and less skilled than most of the crew. I fetch materials, fit things under supervision and ask someone experienced to check my work; today I had to redo the marking for a row of sockets. I like making something real, but I hate feeling everyone is waiting while I work out the next step.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening around the job and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas works in a school kitchen, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My wage is low, we have about two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few similar electrical jobs nearby. I sometimes use an AI note tool after a colleague has shown me it works, but I never treat an answer as permission to do work beyond my training. I think people should get paid time to learn, not be told to buy their own way out of every change.

say: I'd welcome **quieter change** so juniors have space to learn electrical basics properly.
I'd ask the firm to protect **paid practice** instead of expecting another app to make learning faster.
think: I'd still count the days between **wages and mortgage**, even if the electrical work carried on.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot comfortably cover children's needs alongside an unexpected household repair.
do: Continue **supervised repairs** and ask for checks rather than work beyond training.
Replace bought **yard lunches** with food from home in the first year, using the difference for ordinary bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a tight household account, with only a little relief from the quieter AI picture.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future wouldn't make our mortgage quieter.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** comes from low wages and a thin household reserve, not an expectation that the plateau eliminates all work.
She asks for **paid practice** without counting an unagreed arrangement as available training, and keeps safety checks within her junior role.

steps.text: Continue supervised electrical repairs and request needed checks
Replace bought yard lunches with food brought from home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quieter AI story would give us space to do the basics properly. Nobody learns safe work faster because an office buys another app. I'd still want the juniors' practice time protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work might carry on, but I'd still be counting the days between wages and the mortgage payment. Two weeks of expenses isn't much when a child needs shoes and the boiler makes a noise. A quiet AI future wouldn't make our mortgage quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep turning up for the supervised repair work and asking for the checks I need. In the first plateau year I'd stop buying lunches near the yard and bring food from home, putting the difference towards ordinary bills. I'd ask the supervisor for one paid practice period each week, without pretending it was already agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even without a big AI change. I'd feel a bit less watched by the future, but the household account would still be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the bought lunches before the children's school things. It's a small amount, not a secret plan to build a fortune. I wouldn't tell Tomas that sandwiches solved our money problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask for practice if the supervisor was busy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I need to get this right and ask when someone could watch me practise. I wouldn't do unfamiliar live work alone to prove I deserved the wage. Being older than another junior doesn't make me more qualified.

say: I'd ask what happens to **paid learning** when office tasks move into software.
I'd back a **joint crew request** for clear hours and practice, rather than hide each junior's worry.
think: Pressure for more jobs could leave experienced workers less time to teach me, despite continued **hands-on demand**.
I could remain on **low pay** longer while the mortgage and children's bills carry on arriving.
do: Join the **workers' association** and support a shared request for named paid practice without reduced site pay.
Try the proven **note assistant** during paid work in the first year, with the supervisor checking records.
feel: **Anxious** about remaining at the bottom, while willing to learn a checked tool with real support.
S1.quote: I couldn't buy hours to practise with money we don't have.
fieldNote: Her **collective action** is an actual association membership and shared request, not merely asking a colleague an individual question.
She distinguishes **tool learning** from a course she hasn't enrolled in and keeps any practice conditional on maintained paid hours.

steps.text: Join workers association with other juniors to seek paid practice without reduced site pay
Try the proven note assistant during paid work with supervisor checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should tell us what happens to paid learning when software takes the office tasks. I'd back a joint request from the crew for clear hours and practice time. I'd rather ask together than watch each junior pretend not to be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My practical tasks still need hands, but I worry the experienced people will be pushed through more jobs and have less time to teach me. That could leave me stuck on low pay for longer. The mortgage doesn't wait for a slow learner to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the local workers' association and ask other juniors to put a shared request for protected paid practice to the owner. During the first year I'd try the proven note assistant with my supervisor checking the record, only during paid work. If those practice periods weren't agreed, I'd keep asking rather than claim I'd started a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about getting trapped at the bottom, rather than expecting a robot to walk in next week. I could learn a checked tool. I couldn't buy hours to practise with money we don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would protected practice mean in concrete terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one named period a week with an experienced person assigned, not a vague promise to ask whenever things were quiet. I'd also ask that taking it didn't cut paid site hours. Otherwise the help would come out of the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner rejected the shared request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be disappointed, but I'd keep the association conversation going and ask what other support actually existed. I wouldn't tell the children I was leaving the job in protest. We need the wage while I find a real alternative.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031, without promising that the gap protects junior paid hours.
I'd want the employer and **workers' association** discussing paid routes before the change arrives.
think: I expect to lose a **large share of hours** as the firm prepares for robots and concentrates work on stronger workers.
That loss would threaten the **mortgage**, even if my partner kept the kitchen wage.
do: Ask the association about actual **support eligibility** and mortgage hardship options now, without assuming help is granted.
Enroll in pre-2028 **training** only with covered fees and an intact site wage.
Apply after 2028 for posted **supervised maintenance** jobs, requiring written terms that cover the household gap after travel.
feel: **Alarmed** by an expected large wage loss, with practical enquiries but fear that keeps her awake.
S2.quote: A list of job applications wouldn't stop me waking in the night.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows an expected large personal wage loss and explicit sleep disruption, rather than the robot date alone.
She preserves **eligibility and funding uncertainty** for support, mortgage options, training fees and maintained site pay instead of counting promised help.

steps.text: Ask the association about support eligibility and mortgage hardship options
Enroll in training only with covered fees and an intact site wage
Apply after 2028 for posted supervised maintenance jobs covering household gap after travel in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking change in 2028 comes before the hands-on robots around 2031. That gives us a gap, but it doesn't guarantee a junior enough paid work to finish learning. I'd want the employer and the workers' association talking now about paid routes through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect juniors like me to lose a big share of our paid hours as the firm prepared for robots and kept the strongest workers busy. That would put the mortgage in danger, even if Tomas kept his kitchen wage. I can picture lying awake working out which payment could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the workers' association for help checking what household support and mortgage hardship arrangements we might qualify for, without assuming an answer. I'd ask the firm about paid training before 2028 and enroll only if fees were covered and my site wage stayed intact. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted supervised maintenance vacancies, staying in the present job until the written offer covered the household gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I'm expecting a large loss of my wage in that picture, not just a difficult app. I'd still have forms to fill and jobs to ask about. A list of job applications wouldn't stop me waking in the night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home about the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas what hours I expected to lose and put the mortgage statement on the table. I'd ask the lender what was possible before missing a payment, not promise the family that a pause existed. The children would hear that we were making a plan, not that the house was already safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a supervised maintenance vacancy usable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't leave for an advert saying only that training was available. I'd need the wage, supervised duties, hours and start date in writing. If the offer didn't cover enough of the gap after travel, I'd keep the current wage while looking.

say: I'd use **five years** for proper junior learning while wages still come in.
I'd keep asking together for **paid practice** rather than send everyone home to solve the change alone.
think: More time gives me a chance to become **properly useful** before the biggest work changes.
Today's **mortgage and thin reserve** still make me anxious, even with a later technology date.
do: Continue **home-packed lunches** and the shared request for protected paid practice now.
Take a practical **evening course** before 2031 only with funded fees and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2031 for posted **supervised repair jobs** only where written pay improves after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about current household money, with less pressure from the learning timeline than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Extra years wouldn't put extra money in the account tonight.
fieldNote: She retains **present money anxiety** even while recognising that a longer preparation period could improve competence.
Her **course action** depends on both funded fees and maintained paid hours; without them she would enquire rather than enroll.

steps.text: Continue bringing lunch from home instead of buying near the yard
Maintain the shared request for protected paid practice
Take an evening course only with funded fees and maintained paid hours
Apply for posted supervised repair jobs with better pay after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be used to let the juniors learn properly while wages still come in. I'd still ask together for paid practice, not tell everyone to fix themselves after work. The robots around 2034 would still be part of the same future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have more chance to become useful before the work changed most. But I would still be anxious about this month's mortgage and having only two weeks of expenses. Extra years wouldn't put extra money in the account tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the lunches from home and the shared request for paid practice. I'd take a practical evening course before 2031 only if fees were funded and my paid hours were maintained. In the first year after 2031 I'd review posted supervised repair jobs with the association's help and apply if the written pay was better after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more breathing room about learning but the same thin household buffer. I'd feel less cornered by the technology date than in 2028. I wouldn't sleep like somebody with a year's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to achieve in those extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise the tasks the supervisor had actually cleared me to do and keep asking for checks on the rest. I'd want to become properly competent, not just able to say I had attended a course. The children's homework table isn't a safe substitute for a practical training place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no fee funding or protected hours were available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enroll and pretend it was affordable. I'd ask the association what funded options actually existed and keep the wage I had. A refusal would change the plan, not remove the mortgage payment.

say: I'd ask the firm to use **a decade** for paid junior development with clear supervision.
I'd want **paid places**, rather than years of encouraging messages before thinking AI and later robots arrive.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still need income when robots followed around 2039.
Older children wouldn't guarantee cheap living, and today's **low pay** and thin reserve would still worry me.
do: Maintain the **association request** and ask for a written paid development plan at the work review.
Take a practical **course** before 2036 only with funded fees and maintained wages.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair roles** matching completed skills and offering better pay after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with less dread about rushed learning and no assumed retirement income.
S4.quote: Ten years is too long to live on a promise of a practice session.
fieldNote: She makes **no pension assumption** from being in her fifties and doesn't assume older children eliminate household costs.
Her **yearly check** looks for learning actually provided and resulting pay, with real vacancies considered if promises remain empty.

steps.text: Maintain the association request for protected paid development
Take a practical course only with funded fees and maintained wages
Apply for posted repair roles matching completed skills and improving take-home pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the firm time to stop treating junior learning as a favour. I'd still want paid places and clear supervision, not ten years of encouraging messages. Thinking work in 2036 and robots around 2039 would be a long enough warning to organise properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change and about 56 when the robots followed, not automatically ready to stop earning. The children would be older, but I can't count on that making the mortgage or household cheap. Right now I would still have low pay and two weeks of bills behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the association request going and ask for a written paid development plan at my work review. I'd take a practical course before 2036 only with fee funding and maintained wages. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair roles that matched my actual completed skills and offered better pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money today, with less dread about being hurried through learning. I could imagine becoming a capable worker over that time. I wouldn't turn that hope into a claim that retirement would cover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about your own learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them learning at 43 is slow some days, but I'm still doing it. I wouldn't make them responsible for fixing our future wages or choose their studies around this card. I would want them to see that asking for help at work isn't shameful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that the decade was being used well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each year what I'd actually been allowed to learn and what that did to my pay. If the answer stayed nothing, I'd look at actual vacancies sooner rather than wait for 2036. Ten years is too long to live on a promise of a practice session.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose a large part of the wage before I had become good enough to move. Funded practical training with wages kept intact would help, and someone to check what mortgage support we actually qualified for. I need learning time that doesn't come out of the children's dinner money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the junior is also the parent doing the evening meals and homework. I can't create a spare working day after everyone goes to bed. People can want to learn and still need the hours and money made possible.

headlineQuote: I need learning time that doesn't come out of the children's dinner money.
portrait: **Priya, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, learning more slowly than the skilled crew and earning low pay.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and only two weeks of expenses saved near few alternative employers.
She uses AI **occasionally after proof**, insists on supervision and favours collective requests for paid learning rather than private unfunded effort.
The fast picture brings **alarm** over expected wage loss; longer timelines ease learning pressure without erasing current mortgage anxiety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens a large wage loss before she becomes skilled enough to move into better work.
whatWouldHelp: Funded **practical training** with maintained wages would make learning possible.
Help checking actual **mortgage support eligibility** would clarify household options without assuming assistance exists.
